issues.issue: The notice states terrorism insurance is 'made available' under the Act, while the same disclosure states the premium attributable to terrorism coverage is $-0- (c010). A court could be asked whether terrorism coverage was in fact purchased.

The definition strings together certification, violence, damage-location and coercive-purpose elements with semicolons and a single 'and', leaving unclear whether all elements are independently required or merely descriptive of the Secretary's certification.

A zero terrorism premium sits against the disclosure in c005 that the policy 'makes available' terrorism insurance with no terrorism exclusion or sublimit. The two could be read as inconsistent about whether the peril is covered.

This recital-like notice describes Executive Liability, EPL and Fiduciary coverage sections, none of which appear in Item 3 Coverage Summary (c020), which lists only General Terms, Crime and Special Coverage. A court could be asked what, if anything, it operates on.
It describes claims-made triggers for coverage sections not purchased under Item 3 (c020), and cannot be squared with the Crime Coverage Section's discovery-based trigger in Exclusion 19 (c115).

The extended reporting period is described only for claims-made sections not included in Item 3 Coverage Summary (c020); it has no counterpart in the Crime section's 60-day post-termination discovery rule (c115).

This Declarations legend describes claims-made coverage sections and defense-costs erosion, yet the only coverage purchased per Item 3 (c020) is Crime/Special Coverage, which has no 'Defense Costs' or 'Claim' mechanism. Its application to this policy is uncertain.
The policy period runs 'To 42:01 A.M.', an impossible time and a plain mechanical error for 12:01 A.M. The expiry moment is therefore not stated correctly on the face of the Declarations.
'SPECIAL COVERAGE' is listed as a purchased coverage with no accompanying definition or coverage section text in the instrument.

Item 3 lists a 'SPECIAL COVERAGE' section, but the Schedule of Forms attaches a Kidnap/Ransom & Extortion Coverage Section instead, and no Special Coverage section appears. The two cannot be reconciled on the face of the policy.

Item 4 designates prior policy number 8212-1392, the same number as the present policy, which Subsection 12 (c047) then terminates as of inception. A court could be asked which instrument is terminated.

Worldwide territory sits against the Compliance With Applicable Trade Sanction Laws endorsement (c058), which withdraws coverage wherever sanctions laws prohibit it. The reach of the worldwide grant is therefore qualified elsewhere.

This priority rule is the instrument's own conflict-resolution tool, and its operation is tested by the several endorsements that amend the same Crime provisions (c149 and c156 both rewrite Exclusion 19). Its ordering of endorsements against coverage-section text is not spelled out.

'Claim' is left to the applicable coverage section, but the Crime Coverage Section's Definitions (Subsection 11) contain no definition of Claim, while the notice provisions (c031) and the Late Notice endorsement (c050) turn on that term. The definition points to a meaning that does not exist for the only coverage purchased.

Notice here is keyed to a 'Claim', but the Crime section conditions coverage on notice of Discovery of loss within ninety days (c136), and defines no Claim at all. Which notice regime governs a crime loss is left unresolved.

This excuse for late notice sits against Subsection 27 of the Crime section (c136), which makes notice within ninety days of Discovery an express condition precedent to coverage. The two set different consequences for the same failure.

The conversion date here (judgment final, settlement agreed, loss due) differs from the Crime section's rule fixing the rate on the day the loss is Discovered (c139), though the opening words 'except as otherwise provided' may harmonise them.
'Full compliance with all the terms of this policy' as a condition precedent is undefined in scope, leaving open whether any breach, however immaterial, bars suit.

Paragraph (f) directs the reader to 'paragraph (g) of this Subsection 11', but no paragraph (g) is lettered in the text; the sub-paragraph lettering (c), (d), (e), (f) is also detached from the text it introduces. The cross-reference cannot be followed as written.
'Customary short rates' is not defined anywhere in the policy and supplies no ascertainable method of computing the refund.

This terminates prior Company bonds at inception, while Subsection 24 Liability for Prior Losses (c125-c127) preserves coverage for losses sustained under those prior bonds; the Conversion endorsement then deletes Subsection 24 altogether.

This endorsement makes late notice fatal only where the Company is prejudiced, while Subsection 27 of the Crime section (c136) makes notice within ninety days of Discovery a condition precedent without any prejudice requirement. The endorsement also speaks only of a 'Claim', a term the Crime section never defines.

This restates the General Terms excuse for impossible notice (c033) but is expressly carved out of the prejudice rule in paragraph (1) (c050), leaving the interaction of the two excuses to be worked out.
A direct action by an injured claimant is permitted here, whereas Subsection 8 (c036) bars any person or entity from proceeding against the Company except after an unsatisfied judgment.
'Trade or economic sanctions or other similar laws or regulations' places an undefined catch-all against two named specifics, leaving the reach of 'other similar laws' uncertain.

Insuring Clause 7 is captioned 'Money Orders And Counterfeit Fraud Coverage' in the Declarations, omitting 'Currency' from the defined term 'Money Orders And Counterfeit Currency Fraud' used in the coverage section.
The lettered list (A)-(J) is separated from the column of limits in c063, so which limit attaches to which Insuring Clause is not stated on the face of the Declarations.

Item 4 names 'Medidate Solutions, Inc.' — a misspelling of the insured named in Item 1 — and adds 'and its subsidiaries' without using the defined term Subsidiary. The identity and reach of the designated Organization is therefore uncertain.
Organization is defined by reference to this Item 4 (c098) and Subsidiary is separately defined (c105); the loose phrase 'and its subsidiaries' may or may not import that definition.

This bare column of amounts is not tied to the lettered Insuring Clauses in Item 2 (c061), yet Subsection 25 (c130) allocates liability by reference to 'Item 2(A)' through '2(J)'. The mapping must be inferred.

A single unallocated retention figure sits against provisions applying retentions clause-by-clause (c132) and disapplying them for Insuring Clause 10 (c075) and ERISA Plan loss (c121). Which losses bear the $50,000 is not stated in Item 3 itself.
'Direct loss ... resulting from Theft or Forgery' leaves the directness requirement undefined, a phrase regularly contested in fidelity coverage.
This clause covers loss sustained by 'an Insured', while every other Insuring Clause is keyed to 'an Organization' and Subsection 20 (c116) restricts liability to property of the Organization.

The grant covers 'direct loss ... resulting from Forgery or alteration of a Financial Instrument', then adds an 'including' list confined to checks, drafts and payroll orders; whether the general grant reaches instruments unlike those specifics, and whether an electronic instruction can be a forged Financial Instrument, is genuinely open.

The clause depends on the definitions of Forgery (c089) and Financial Instrument (c088), which speak of the 'signing of the name of another' and of a 'check, draft or similar written promise', and which may not fit the electronic conduct the clause is invoked against.

'Direct loss ... resulting from Computer Fraud committed by a Third Party' turns on both the undefined 'direct' requirement and the borrowed definition of Computer Fraud; whether a fraudulently induced transfer authorised by the insured's own employees is a 'direct loss' from a third party's act is genuinely contestable.

Its reach depends on Computer Violation (c080) and Computer System (c079), and it must also be read against Exclusion 12(k) (c108) and the Privacy and Data Breach endorsement (c146), whose carve-back preserves only Insuring Clause 6.

'Direct loss of Money or Securities ... resulting from Funds Transfer Fraud' incorporates a definition requiring instructions issued 'without such Organization's knowledge or consent', and it is genuinely arguable whether a transfer executed by deceived but authorised employees qualifies.

The Privacy and Data Breach endorsement (c146) expressly preserves only loss 'otherwise covered under Insuring Clause 6', which affects how this clause is read alongside the excluded computer/privacy losses.

Credit Card Fraud is defined (c082) as the forgery or alteration of a written instrument, yet Exclusion 18 (c114) removes coverage under this Insuring Clause for loss caused by 'any forgery or alteration of, on or in any written instrument'. The grant and the exclusion largely cancel each other absent the provisos.

The final sentence disapplies any retention to Insuring Clause 10 expenses, while Subsection 25 (c132) states the Company's liability applies only to loss in excess of the Item 3 Retention. The two rules must be reconciled.

'The unlawful taking or the fraudulently induced transfer of Money, Securities or Property resulting from a Computer Violation' is open to a narrow reading (hacking that itself moves funds) and a broad one (any transfer induced by manipulated computer data). The causal link 'resulting from' does not resolve which.

Its content is wholly dependent on Computer Violation (c080) and Computer System (c079), and it must be squared with the Privacy and Data Breach endorsement (c146), which excludes computer-based losses except those under Insuring Clause 6.

'Owned and operated or leased and operated by an Organization' leaves unclear whether third-party hosted or cloud-based facilities used by the insured fall within the Computer System, an ambiguity central to any computer-fraud claim.

'The fraudulent entry of Data into ... a Computer System' and 'change to Data elements' are susceptible to a narrow reading (unauthorised manipulation of the system) and a broad one (any deceptive data, such as spoofed message content, entering the system). The trailing words 'directed against an Organization' add a further undefined requirement.
The definition operates only through Computer Fraud (c078) and Computer System (c079), whose 'owned and operated' limitation may exclude the very facilities into which the data is entered.
This defines Credit Card Fraud as forgery or alteration of a written instrument, the very thing Exclusion 18 (c114) excludes from Insuring Clause 8. Read together the grant is nearly self-cancelling.

'A representation of information, knowledge, facts, concepts or instructions which are processed and stored in a Computer System' is broad enough to cover ordinary message content, and its boundary against mere communications is not drawn.

'Facts which would cause a reasonable person to assume that a loss ... has occurred' fixes the discovery trigger by an undefined reasonableness standard, and the alternative limb ('acts ... that may subsequently result in a loss') is broader still.
The definition turns on 'regular service', compensation by Salary and the right to 'govern and direct', boundaries that are contested whenever contractors or seconded staff are involved.
Subparagraph (a) is replaced in its entirety by Endorsement No. 1 (c143), which adds 'trustee'; the base text remains in the printed policy, so the operative list must be taken from the endorsement.

'A check, draft or similar written promise, order or direction to pay a sum certain in Money' leaves open whether an electronic payment instruction or e-mail direction is a 'similar written' instrument, and the general words follow two paper specifics.

'The signing of the name of another natural person or organization' is ambiguous as applied to electronically generated identifiers, and the carve-out for 'a signature that includes, in whole or in part, one's own name' pulls the other way; the final sentence equating electronic reproductions with handwriting deepens the doubt.
The definition drives Insuring Clause 4 (c069) and Credit Card Fraud (c082), and its 'electronically produced' sentence sits uneasily with the requirement of a written Financial Instrument (c088).

'Fraudulent ... instructions ... purportedly issued by an Organization ... without such Organization's knowledge or consent' is ambiguous where the transfer instruction is actually given by the insured's own deceived employees; 'knowledge or consent' can be read as to the instruction or as to the fraud.
The parenthetical 'other than Forgery' carves this definition against Forgery (c089) and Insuring Clause 4 (c069), so a single fraudulent instruction may fall between the two grants.

Insured is limited to Organizations plus (for Insuring Clause 1) plans, yet Insuring Clause 1 (c066) pays for loss sustained by 'an Insured' while the other clauses use 'an Organization', and Subsection 20 (c116) restricts liability to the Organization's property.

'Currency, coin, bank notes and bullion' is a closed list of physical items, leaving open whether funds held or transferred electronically are Money for the purposes of the funds-transfer and computer-fraud grants.
Organization is defined solely by Item 4 of the Crime Declarations, which misnames the insured as 'Medidate Solutions, Inc.' and adds an undefined reference to 'its subsidiaries' (c062).

Defining Property as 'tangible property other than Money or Securities' leaves electronic assets and funds outside all three defined categories in some readings, which matters wherever the loss is intangible.
The definition reads 'negotiable and nor-negotiable instruments', a mechanical error for 'non-negotiable' that on its face changes the class of instruments described.

Defining Third Party negatively as anyone other than an Employee or a person 'acting in collusion with an Employee' leaves 'collusion' undefined, so a deceived employee's participation may or may not defeat third-party status.

Exclusion 12(n) removes loss due to listed frauds 'or other fraudulent, dishonest or criminal act ... committed by any authorized representative of an Insured'; both the catch-all after the enumerated frauds and the undefined 'authorized representative' leave the exclusion's reach uncertain.

Sub-paragraph (b) (loss of trade secrets or confidential information) is deleted and replaced by the Privacy and Data Breach endorsement (c146), so the printed list of exclusions no longer states the operative terms.

'Any agent, broker, factor, commission merchant, consignee, contractor, independent contractor, subcontractor or other similar representative' ends in a catch-all whose reach against the enumerated specifics is uncertain, particularly against the Employee definition that includes leased and temporary staff.

'Kidnap, ransom or other extortion payment (as distinct from Robbery) surrendered to any person as a result of a threat' does not say how a fraudulently induced payment is distinguished from an extorted one.

Exclusion 17 is deleted in its entirety by Endorsement No. 4 to the Crime section, yet the printed exclusion remains in the policy text; the operative position on Insuring Clause 5 losses can only be read from the endorsement.

This exclusion removes from Insuring Clause 8 loss caused by 'any forgery or alteration of, on or in any written instrument' — precisely what the definition of Credit Card Fraud (c082) requires for the coverage to attach, leaving the grant nearly nullified apart from the two provisos.

Exclusion 19 is rewritten 'in its entirety' twice over by endorsements effective the same date — the Conversion endorsement (c149), which drops the 60-day notice requirement and adds a discovery-before-termination test, and the Amend Exclusion 19 endorsement (c156), which keeps it. The printed exclusion cannot be reconciled with both.
Liability is limited to property owned by or held by 'the Organization', while Insuring Clause 1 (c066) pays for loss sustained by 'an Insured', a term that includes ERISA and Non-ERISA Plans.

The ERISA version of Insuring Clause 1 covers 'a fraudulent or dishonest act', a materially wider trigger than the defined Theft or Forgery used in the clause it replaces, and 'dishonest' is left undefined.

This deletes 'sixty (60) days' wherever it appears in Exclusion 19, but the Conversion endorsement's replacement Exclusion 19 (c149) contains no such words at all, while the Amend Exclusion 19 endorsement (c156) reinstates them. The instruction cannot be applied coherently.
The blanket disapplication of any retention for ERISA Plan loss sits against Subsection 25 (c132), which makes liability apply only to loss in excess of the Item 3 Retention.

This first paragraph is replaced 'in its entirety' by the Conversion endorsement (c150), which converts the trigger from coverage 'after the effective date' of acquisition to coverage for loss 'Discovered after' it; the printed text no longer states the operative rule.

'Such information as the Company in its sole discretion may require' and 'any reasonable additional premium required by the Company', with automatic voidance for failure, are one-sided and leave the insured's obligation without an ascertainable limit.

Subsection 24 is deleted in its entirety by paragraph (3) of the Conversion endorsement, which also deletes all references to it; the printed text therefore contradicts the operative policy, and Subsection 25 (c128) still opens 'Subject to Subsection 24'.
This paragraph forms part of Subsection 24, which the Conversion endorsement deletes in its entirety, while Subsection 12 (c047) separately terminates prior Company bonds at inception.
This limitation belongs to Subsection 24, which paragraph (3) of the Conversion endorsement deletes in its entirety, leaving no prior-loss limit to apply.

It is expressly 'Subject to Subsection 24', which the Conversion endorsement deletes, and it is itself replaced by paragraph (4) of that endorsement (c151), which shifts the trigger from loss sustained during the Policy Period to loss Discovered during the Policy Period.
'Any series of related acts, casualties or events' and acts in which the same Third Party is 'concerned or implicated' set the aggregation boundary in language whose limits are not defined.
The single Retention applies to 'each loss', while Insuring Clause 10 (c075) and the ERISA provision (c121) disapply any retention and Item 3 (c064) states one unallocated figure.
Imputing all knowledge to all Insureds sits against the Discovery definition (c084), which confines discovery to an Executive or Insurance Representative and excludes knowledge of a complicit one.
'At the earliest practicable moment' is a vague standard laid alongside the fixed ninety-day and six-month outer limits, leaving unclear when the condition precedent is actually breached.

Making notice an unqualified condition precedent cannot be squared with the New York Late Notice endorsement (c050), which provides that late notice does not invalidate coverage absent prejudice, or with Subsection 5 of the General Terms (c033).
The lettered sub-paragraphs (a) and (b) are printed detached from the text that follows them, so which limitation period attaches to which claim is not clear from the provision as written.
Valuation is fixed by reference to the day of Discovery, whereas Subsection 6 of the General Terms (c034) fixes foreign-currency conversion at the date loss is due or judgment becomes final.

Saying the coverage section is 'null and void' to the extent of other collectible insurance, then providing that it 'shall cover such loss' in excess of that insurance, states the same rule in two inconsistent registers.
It overlaps Exclusion 12(m) (c108), which addresses the same excess-of-other-recovery position for property in the custody of banks and carriers by a different mechanism.
It replaces subparagraph (a) of the Executive definition, but the unamended text (c087) remains printed in the coverage section, so the operative list of Executives appears twice in different forms.

'Any similar type of nonpublic information' follows a list running from patents to health information, and 'loss involving the disclosure ... or use of' confidential information has no stated boundary; how far the catch-all reaches beyond the enumerated categories is genuinely open.

The carve-back preserves only loss 'otherwise covered under Insuring Clause 6, Funds Transfer Fraud Coverage', leaving the Computer Fraud grant in Insuring Clause 5 (c070) exposed to an exclusion broad enough to swallow it.

This replacement Exclusion 19 requires loss to be sustained and Discovered before termination, with no post-termination notice window, while the Amend Exclusion 19 endorsement (c156), effective the same date, rewrites the same exclusion 'in its entirety' with a 60-day post-termination discovery and notice regime. Both cannot govern.

It rewrites the first paragraph of Subsection 23 so that new subsidiaries are covered only for loss 'Discovered after' the acquisition, displacing the printed text (c123) which grants coverage after the effective date of the acquisition.

It converts the trigger to loss Discovered during the Policy Period, contradicting the printed Subsection 25 (c128), which limits liability to loss sustained during the Policy Period, and sitting against the Amended Exclusion 19 (c156), which allows discovery within sixty days after termination.

'All other terms ... remain unchanged' has to operate alongside a further endorsement (c156) that changes one of the very provisions this endorsement rewrote, so which endorsement survives is left to construction.

This rewrites Exclusion 19 'in its entirety' to require Discovery and written notice within sixty days after termination, while the Conversion endorsement (c149), effective the same date, rewrites the same exclusion in its entirety to require discovery before termination with no notice window. The policy contains two irreconcilable versions of Exclusion 19.
'All other terms ... remain unchanged' does not resolve its relationship with the Conversion endorsement (c149), which had already replaced the same Exclusion 19 in different terms.
